method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: Friday's strong jobs report gave the dollar its best day since June, and it gave some back on Monday as hopes for US–Iran talks calmed markets. On Tuesday Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said he will back a December rate rise even if inflation cools, and markets now see about an 85% chance, so the dollar firmed ahead of the October inflation figures due later that day.

EUR.text: The euro fell to about $1.115 on Friday after a strong US jobs report, then climbed back to about $1.12 on Monday as the dollar eased. At home, shop sales fell far more than expected in September and the European Central Bank's chief economist Philip Lane sounded cautious, so a December rate rise looks less certain even with inflation near 4%.

GBP.text: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% last Thursday, its first rise since 2023, and the pound edged up to about $1.34 on Monday as the dollar eased. In his first speech since, Governor Andrew Bailey said AI is starting to lift UK growth but gave no hint on December, so Thursday's UK growth figures matter more.

JPY.text: The yen is near 158 per dollar, held down by a likely Federal Reserve rate rise in December that Fed Governor Christopher Waller backed again on Tuesday. Notes from the Bank of Japan's October meeting show some members want faster rate rises, and cheaper oil eases Japan's import bill, but very weak household spending argues for going slowly.

CHF.text: The franc drew safe-haven money last week as stocks sold off, and weekend attacks on tankers near Hormuz plus tougher talk from Iran's Revolutionary Guards keep war risk alive as markets reopen. Softer words from both Washington and Tehran on Sunday about a deal take a little of that away, and Swiss inflation at 1.5% makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to justify.

CAD.text: Canada lost jobs for a second month in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%, which weakens the case for another Bank of Canada rate rise. Oil, Canada's biggest export, kept falling and briefly went below $90 a barrel on Tuesday as fears of new US strikes on Iran faded.

AUD.text: Australian consumer confidence fell to a four-year low in November as the 4.85% cash rate and high living costs bite, which makes another Reserve Bank of Australia rate rise less likely. China, Australia's biggest customer, bought far more from abroad than expected in October, a mild sign of firmer demand, so the Australian dollar has pulls both ways.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar led the major currencies on Monday, up about 1.5% to near 56 US cents, as calmer markets and Saturday's election, which left Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's three-party bloc just ahead, gave it some relief. About 400,000 votes are still to count, so who governs may not be clear until November 27, and the jobless rate is already at its highest since 2015. Stronger-than-expected Chinese imports in October are a small extra help.

XAU.text: Gold climbed back to about $4,130 an ounce on Monday as cheaper oil eased inflation fears. But on Tuesday Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller backed a December rate rise whatever October inflation shows, which weighs on gold, so the US inflation figures later that day are the big test.

OIL.text: Brent crude fell 16% last week, almost 6% more on Monday, and briefly slipped under $90 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since August, after President Trump said more strikes on Iran weren't needed and the war could end soon. Attacks on ships near Hormuz have not stopped, so the drop could reverse quickly if talks stall.

items.headline: Fed's Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in London that he will back a December rate rise even if October inflation cools, and that a half-point rise should be on the table if underlying prices climb fast.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising interest rates to fight inflation that is running well above its 2% goal, and markets already saw a December rise as likely after a strong US jobs report last Friday.
beats.happened: Speaking on Tuesday, hours before the US October inflation figures, Waller said he would support a quarter-point rise at the December 8–9 meeting even if inflation improves on September. He added that a half-point rise should be considered if core prices, which leave out food and energy, rise 0.3% or more in the month; economists expect about 0.2%. He called inflation his main focus and brushed off recent stock market falls.
beats.means: One of the Fed's most influential voices has all but committed to a December rise before seeing the data, and opened the door to a bigger step. Markets moved the chance of a December rise to about 85%, so a soft inflation figure later on Tuesday would now do less to change the plan.
beats.fx: Firmer rate-rise talk supports the US dollar, which rose against most currencies after his remarks, and weighs on the yen and gold, which pay no or little interest.

impact.why: A senior Fed official backed a December rate rise whatever October inflation shows, and raised the idea of a bigger one.
A wider gap between US and Japanese interest rates keeps the yen near 158 per dollar.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures: core prices up 0.3% or more would make a half-point December rise a live option; a clearly softer reading would test how firm Waller's backing is.

items.headline: Brent falls below $90 a barrel for the first time since August
items.story_title: US–Iran: talk of a deal pulls oil off its war highs
items.summary: Brent crude briefly dropped under $90 a barrel on Tuesday, its lowest since August, after President Trump said more strikes on Iran weren't needed and the war could end soon.

beats.was: Oil had jumped this autumn on the US–Iran war and attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route that carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Brent, the main world benchmark, already fell almost 6% on Monday.
beats.happened: After meeting Qatar's Prime Minister at the White House on Monday, Trump said further military action against Iran didn't seem very necessary and that the war should end fairly soon. Brent slipped briefly below $90 on Tuesday and US crude fell to about $85, before both won back part of the drop later in the morning.
beats.means: Traders are removing the extra price they had paid for the risk of a wider war and blocked supplies. That eases the inflation worry from energy, but the drop could reverse quickly, as ships near the strait are still being attacked.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil is a drag on the Canadian dollar, as oil is Canada's biggest export, and a help to the yen, since Japan buys almost all its energy abroad.

impact.why: Brent fell below $90 for the first time since August as fears of more US strikes on Iran faded.
Lower oil prices cut into Canada's main export earnings.
Cheaper oil shrinks Japan's import bill.

items.watch: Whether US–Iran talks produce a deal, and any new attacks on ships near Hormuz that would bring the war premium back.

items.headline: Oil keeps sliding in Asia as fears of new US strikes on Iran fade; Brent near $92
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Brent crude traded near $92 a barrel early Tuesday in Asia after settling almost 6% lower on Monday, and Gulf producers are cutting prices to win buyers as ships start moving through Hormuz again.

beats.was: The war with Iran shut most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, and pushed Brent well above $100. Last week it fell 16% on hopes of a deal.
beats.happened: President Trump played down the chance of new US strikes on Iran, and Brent settled Monday at about $92.57, down $5.75, then slipped to about $92.25 in early Asian trade. US crude was near $87. Middle Eastern producers are cutting their selling prices as flows through Hormuz recover, even though attacks on ships nearby continue.
beats.means: Price cuts by Gulf sellers suggest supply is coming back faster than buyers expected, which adds to fears of too much oil. A new attack or a stall in talks could still reverse the drop quickly.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs on the Canadian dollar and helps big oil importers like Japan.

impact.why: Brent extended its slide as strike fears faded and Gulf sellers cut prices.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export earnings.
A smaller oil bill eases pressure on Japan's trade balance.

items.watch: Any confirmed progress in US–Iran talks, or a fresh attack on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: China's October imports jump 41.6%, far more than expected, while exports beat forecasts and the trade surplus shrinks
items.story_title: China trade: AI-led export boom, imports picking up
items.summary: China's exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier in October and imports rose 41.6%, well above the 32% expected, so the monthly trade surplus narrowed to about $105 billion.

beats.was: China, the biggest buyer of Australian and New Zealand goods, has been selling record amounts abroad, much of it AI hardware such as memory chips, while buying relatively little, which has kept worries about weak demand at home alive.
beats.happened: Customs figures for October showed exports up 35.2% on a year earlier, a bit above the 33.5% forecast, and imports up 41.6% against a 32% forecast. The surplus fell to about $105 billion from about $134 billion in September, short of the roughly $126 billion expected. For the year so far the surplus is already above $1 trillion.
beats.means: Faster buying from abroad is a sign that demand inside China may be firming, though it's not yet clear how much is higher prices rather than bigger volumes. Strong exports also add to pressure on Beijing over trade imbalances before President Trump meets President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month.
beats.fx: Stronger Chinese imports are mild good news for the Australian and New Zealand dollars, whose economies sell heavily to China.

impact.why: China, Australia's biggest customer, bought much more from abroad than expected.
Firmer Chinese imports help New Zealand's export earnings.

items.watch: The detailed customs figures showing whether imports rose on prices or volumes, and trade talk at the Trump–Xi meeting later this month.

items.headline: Australian consumer confidence falls to a four-year low as higher rates and living costs bite
items.story_title: RBA: is 4.85% the peak?
items.summary: The Westpac–Melbourne Institute measure of Australian consumer confidence fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November, its lowest since late 2022, with mortgage holders at a record low.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008, with inflation at 4.3% and petrol nearing A$2.40 a litre.
beats.happened: The monthly Westpac–Melbourne Institute survey dropped to 78.2 from 80.4, where anything below 100 means pessimists outnumber optimists. Mood among people with a mortgage hit a record low, more than 70% expect mortgage rates to rise further, and households turned gloomy on house prices for the first time since late 2022.
beats.means: Households are feeling the rate rises, which makes it harder for the central bank to keep going. Westpac expects it to hold rates at its December 7–8 meeting and not raise them in February either.
beats.fx: Weaker spending ahead lowers the chance of more rate rises, which takes some support from the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Gloomier households make another Reserve Bank of Australia rate rise less likely.

items.watch: Thursday's Australian jobs figures for October; a strong report would revive talk of another rate rise.

items.headline: Notes from the Bank of Japan's October meeting show some members want faster rate rises
items.story_title: BoJ: a rate rise in December?
items.summary: The Bank of Japan's notes from its October 29–30 meeting show the board now debating how fast to raise rates, not whether, though Japanese household spending fell 6.8% from a year earlier in September.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan has been slowly raising rates from near zero, and markets already expect another rise, to 1.5%, at its December 17–18 meeting. The yen sits near 158 per dollar, close to where Japan's government has stepped in to support it.
beats.happened: The 'Summary of Opinions' from the October meeting said underlying inflation is now broadly in line with the 2% goal. One member said the rate that neither speeds up nor slows the economy is likely well above 1%, and core inflation is seen above 3% toward the end of the fiscal year. More cautious members warned that past rises are still feeding through and that consumer spending is weak. Separate figures showed household spending down 6.8% on a year earlier in September.
beats.means: The board's centre of gravity has moved toward more and possibly quicker rate rises, which backs up December pricing. Weak spending is the main reason some members want to go slowly.
beats.fx: A firmer path of Japanese rate rises gives the yen some support against the pull of higher US rates.

impact.why: Some Bank of Japan members want rates to rise faster than markets expect.

items.watch: Whether Governor Kazuo Ueda or his deputies hint at December; a very soft spending or wage figure could cool the talk.

items.headline: Two Fed presidents warn that inflation is the main risk, with the AI building boom adding to price pressure
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said the rush to build AI data centres is pushing up prices like a surge in demand, and Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said the Fed's path is fairly clear with inflation still high.

beats.was: A strong October jobs report on Friday left markets seeing roughly an 80% chance that the Federal Reserve raises rates at its December 8–9 meeting.
beats.happened: Speaking on Monday, Goolsbee said the cost of land, workers, power and materials for AI projects shows the economy is running into limits, and that services prices are rising in ways oil and tariffs don't explain. Barkin said a healthy economy and stubborn inflation make the Fed's course relatively simple. Both get a vote on rates from January.
beats.means: Neither pushed back on a December rate rise. Their words add to the sense that Fed officials see inflation, not jobs, as the bigger worry.
beats.fx: Firm talk from Fed officials supports the dollar ahead of Tuesday's October inflation figures.

impact.why: Two Fed presidents kept the focus on inflation, backing a possible December rate rise.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures; a soft reading would weaken the case these officials are making.

items.headline: Brent falls almost 5% toward $93 on reports Qatar is carrying an Iranian Hormuz offer to the White House
items.story_title: US–Iran talks: Hormuz reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Brent crude dropped almost 5% on Monday to about $93 a barrel after reports that Qatar's prime minister is taking an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to the White House. Neither Washington nor Tehran has confirmed it.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut since the US–Iran war began in late February. Brent already fell 16% last week, its biggest weekly drop since 2020, on hopes of peace talks.
beats.happened: Reports said Iran would reopen the strait and stop attacks on tankers if the US lifts its naval blockade and frees about $8 billion of Iranian money held in Qatar. Brent fell to about $93 and US crude to under $88. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the two sides are not close to a breakthrough.
beats.means: Markets are pricing a reopening before any deal is signed. If the offer holds, more oil reaches the market and fuel-driven inflation cools; if it falls through, prices could jump back quickly.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs on the Canadian dollar and helps big oil importers such as Japan and the euro area. It also eases inflation fears, which takes some heat off central banks.

impact.why: A possible Hormuz reopening would put more oil back on the market.
Canada earns less when oil, its biggest export, gets cheaper.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a lower price shrinks its import bill.

items.watch: Whether the White House or Iran confirms the terms; a denial or a fresh tanker attack would likely send oil back up.

items.headline: The dollar ends Monday lower against the euro and yen as hopes for US–Iran talks lift appetite for risk
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: By the New York close the dollar had given back about half a percent, with the euro near $1.12 and the New Zealand dollar up about 1.5% to around 56 US cents, as calmer markets drew money away from safe havens.

beats.was: A strong US jobs report on Friday, with 165,000 new jobs in October, gave the dollar its best day since June after a week of selling in AI-linked stocks and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: On Monday stocks bounced, led by technology shares, and a measure of US stock-market fear fell about 10%. Qatar's prime minister met President Trump at the White House as US–Iran talks went on. The dollar index slipped to about 101.8, the euro rose to about $1.120, the pound to about $1.342, and the dollar held near 158 yen.
beats.means: The dollar's Friday jump was partly a flight to safety, and some of that has unwound as fear eases. Markets still see about an 82% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, so the bigger driver for the dollar hasn't changed.
beats.fx: Calmer markets help the New Zealand and Australian dollars most. Tuesday's US October inflation figures decide whether the dollar's slip continues or reverses.

impact.why: The kiwi led the major currencies as fear in markets faded.
The dollar gave back part of Friday's safe-haven jump.
The euro climbed back to about $1.12 as the dollar eased.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures; a firm reading would likely lift the dollar again.

items.headline: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey says AI is starting to lift UK growth, but warns of a bubble in AI shares
items.story_title: Bank of England: rates rise again to fight energy costs
items.summary: In his first speech since last week's rate rise, Bailey said AI looks like an early boost to how much the UK economy can produce, warned that AI share prices could be a bubble, and gave no fresh hint about December.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised its main rate to 4% last Thursday, its first rise since 2023, because the Iran war has kept energy prices high. Markets wanted to hear whether Bailey sees more rises ahead.
beats.happened: Speaking at a lecture in Zurich on Monday, Bailey said AI appears to be raising output without adding to price pressure, and credited it with a sizeable share of UK growth this year. He also warned that AI share prices may run ahead of what the technology delivers, and defended central banks' independence from politicians.
beats.means: Growth that comes from doing more with the same inputs is the kind that cools inflation, which gives the bank less reason to keep raising rates. But Bailey avoided any signal on December, so the next steer comes from data.
beats.fx: No new push for the pound either way. Thursday's UK growth figures for July to September matter more for whether another rate rise comes.

impact.why: Bailey sounded upbeat on growth but gave no new hint on more rate rises.

items.watch: Thursday's UK growth figures and UK inflation data next week; either could revive talk of a December rate rise.

items.headline: US sale of $58 billion in three-year government bonds draws its weakest demand of the year
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: The US Treasury sold $58 billion of three-year notes on Monday at 4.627%, a little above where they traded beforehand, with the lowest demand of 2026 and less buying from overseas.

beats.was: The US sells new government debt every week. How eagerly buyers, especially foreign ones, take it up is a gauge of appetite for US assets, and this week's sales come just before key inflation figures.
beats.happened: Bids covered the sale about 2.5 times, the weakest this year. The yield came in slightly higher than expected, the biggest such gap since May. Foreign-type buyers took a smaller share, while US domestic buyers took a record share.
beats.means: Buyers wanted a bit more pay to hold US debt with inflation figures due and a Fed rate rise likely. Softer foreign demand is worth watching, though one sale doesn't make a trend.
beats.fx: Slightly higher US yields lend the dollar some support, but weaker foreign buying is a mild worry for it. Overall a small, two-sided signal.

impact.why: Yields rose a touch, but foreign demand for US debt was soft.

items.watch: The 10-year and 30-year bond sales later this week; weak demand again would add to the worry about foreign appetite.

items.headline: Americans still expect 3.9% inflation over the next year, while fear of losing jobs hits its highest since 2020
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: The New York Fed's monthly survey of consumers showed people expect prices to rise 3.9% over the next year, unchanged from September, while worry about rising unemployment jumped to its highest since April 2020.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve watches what households expect inflation to be, because those expectations can feed into wages and prices. A December rate rise is seen as likely after Friday's strong jobs report.
beats.happened: In the New York Fed's October Survey of Consumer Expectations, the one-year inflation outlook held at 3.9%, slightly above forecasts; the three-year outlook was 3.3% and the five-year 3.0%. The average chance people gave of higher unemployment a year from now rose to 45.3%.
beats.means: Inflation expectations are stuck near three-year highs, which supports the case for a rate rise. But households are growing more nervous about jobs, which cuts the other way.
beats.fx: A small mixed signal for the dollar: sticky inflation expectations back the Fed's tough line, while job fears are a reason for caution.

impact.why: Inflation expectations stayed high, but worry about jobs rose sharply.

items.watch: Tuesday's October inflation figures will show whether actual prices match what households expect.

items.headline: The dollar gives back some of Friday's jobs-day gain as fears over AI stocks and the Middle East fade
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: The dollar slipped about 0.3% on Monday as calmer stock markets and softer talk on Iran drew money back to riskier currencies. The New Zealand dollar led, up about 1% to near 56 US cents.

beats.was: A strong US jobs report on Friday, with 165,000 new jobs in October, gave the dollar its best day since June, after a week of selling in AI-linked stocks and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: In London trading the dollar index eased to about 101.9. The euro rose to about $1.119, the pound to about $1.341, and the dollar dipped just below 158 yen. Markets still see roughly an 81% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, up slightly from the weekend.
beats.means: This is a breather, not a change of view. Money is moving back into riskier currencies as fear fades, but the case for a December Fed rate rise has not weakened ahead of Tuesday's US inflation figures.
beats.fx: Calmer markets help the New Zealand and Australian dollars and the pound against the US dollar. A firm inflation reading on Tuesday could quickly bring the dollar back.

impact.why: The kiwi led the bounce in riskier currencies as fear in markets eased.
The dollar gave back part of Friday's jump as demand for safety faded.
The pound edged up to about $1.341 as the dollar eased.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures; a firm reading would likely lift the dollar again.

items.headline: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey speaks on Monday, days after the first UK rate rise since 2023
items.story_title: Bank of England: rates rise again to fight energy costs
items.summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey is due to speak later on Monday, his first remarks since the bank raised its rate to 4% last Thursday. Traders want to know whether another rise in December is likely.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised its main rate to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since 2023, and warned more could follow while the Iran war keeps energy prices high. Oil has fallen sharply since then.
beats.happened: A daily market preview lists a speech by Governor Andrew Bailey later on Monday. UK figures for growth in July to September follow on Thursday.
beats.means: This is a preview. Bailey's tone will show whether the bank sees last week's rise as one step or the start of a run, and the drop in oil since then gives him room to sound calmer.
beats.fx: Talk of further rises would support the pound; a hint that one rise is enough, helped by cheaper oil, would take some support away.

impact.why: The pound's next step depends on whether Bailey leans toward another rate rise.

items.watch: Whether Bailey signals a December rate rise, and UK growth figures on Thursday.

items.headline: Brent drops below $97 after its biggest weekly fall since 2020, as Trump plays down new Iran strikes
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 1.5% to near $96.90 a barrel on Monday after a 16% drop last week, as President Trump said fresh US strikes on Iran are very unlikely while talks go on.

beats.was: The war with Iran and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's main oil route, pushed oil well above $100 earlier this year. Hopes of a deal sent it sharply lower last week.
beats.happened: Brent slipped to about $96.90 and US crude to about $89.85 early Monday. Ships were still hit near Hormuz over the weekend, and Yemen's Houthi rebels damaged a Saudi Aramco office in Riyadh, but traders focused on the softer US tone. JPMorgan estimates the world is producing more oil than it uses.
beats.means: The market is betting the war winds down and supply recovers. Fresh attacks show the risk of a new jump has not gone away.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil hurts oil exporters such as Canada and helps big importers such as Japan and the euro area, and it eases inflation worries everywhere.

impact.why: Softer US talk on strikes and signs of a supply surplus pull prices lower.
Lower oil prices cut Canada's export earnings.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so cheaper crude eases its bill.

items.watch: Any new attack on ships near Hormuz, and whether US-Iran talks produce a deal.

items.headline: Japan spent a record $50 billion in one day defending the yen in July, official data show
items.story_title: Japan's fight to prop up the yen
items.summary: Figures from Japan's Ministry of Finance confirm it spent almost 8 trillion yen, about $50 billion, buying yen on July 30, the most ever in a single day.

beats.was: The yen fell to its weakest in about 40 years, near 164 per dollar, earlier this year, because US interest rates are far higher than Japan's. Japan's government buys yen with its dollar reserves when it thinks the fall has gone too far.
beats.happened: New detail from the finance ministry shows a record one-day purchase on July 30, and about 15.4 trillion yen, roughly $97 billion, spent across July and August. The US Treasury joined in that operation, the first joint action of its kind since 1998.
beats.means: This is old spending made public, not a new move. It does remind traders that Tokyo, with Washington's backing, has acted hard before and could again if the yen slides back toward its lows.
beats.fx: The yen sits near 158 per dollar. The record shows there is a line the government will defend, which limits how far sellers dare push it, but the wide gap between US and Japanese rates still pulls the yen down.

impact.why: Proof of heavy past buying makes a further deep fall riskier to bet on.
US support for Japan's buying caps the dollar against the yen, though higher US rates still favour it.

items.watch: Whether the yen weakens back toward 160 per dollar, warnings from Japan's finance minister, and the Bank of Japan's December meeting.

items.headline: China's factory prices rise 5.7% in October while shop prices cool to 0.7%
items.story_title: China: dearer factory costs, weak shoppers
items.summary: Prices charged by Chinese factories rose 5.7% from a year earlier in October, the fastest since mid-2022, while consumer prices rose just 0.7%, a touch below forecasts.

beats.was: China is the biggest buyer of Australian and New Zealand exports, so its economy matters a lot for those currencies. The Iran war has pushed up the cost of fuel and raw materials worldwide.
beats.happened: China's producer price index, which tracks what factories charge, rose 5.7% on the year, above the 5.3% expected and up from 5.0% in September; mining prices were up about 28%. Consumer prices rose 0.7%, below the 0.8% expected and down from 0.9%, as food got cheaper, and core prices slowed to 0.8%.
beats.means: Higher factory prices come mostly from dearer energy and metals, not from strong demand. Shoppers are still spending cautiously, so China's own demand looks soft, while iron ore sits near its lowest since 2022.
beats.fx: Weak Chinese demand and cheap iron ore weigh on the Australian dollar, though high metal prices for copper and others soften the blow. The mix gives no clear push either way.

impact.why: Soft Chinese shoppers and cheap iron ore hurt, but high mining and metal prices help.
Cooling consumer prices point to weak Chinese demand for New Zealand's food exports.

items.watch: China's October trade, lending and activity figures later this month, and the iron ore price.

items.headline: Gold climbs 1.6% to about $4,130 as cheaper oil eases inflation worries
items.story_title: Gold: cheaper oil vs a likely Fed rate rise
items.summary: Gold rose 1.6% to near $4,130 an ounce in Asian trading on Monday, as falling oil prices eased fears of higher inflation. Silver jumped 2.8%.

beats.was: Gold gained about 5% last week, but a strong US jobs report on Friday pushed it down about 1% to near $4,050, because it made a December rate rise by the Federal Reserve more likely. Higher rates hurt gold, which pays no interest.
beats.happened: By early Monday in Asia, gold had climbed back to about $4,130 and silver to about $53. Oil slipped after US President Donald Trump said new strikes on Iran are very unlikely while talks go on, and the US dollar eased a little.
beats.means: Cheaper oil means less inflation pressure, which makes the Fed's rate path look a bit less harsh, and gold benefits. Markets still put the chance of a December Fed rise near 80%, so Tuesday's US inflation figures can quickly undo the gain.
beats.fx: A firmer gold price tends to help the Australian dollar, since Australia is a big gold producer. A hot US inflation reading would likely lift the dollar and push gold back down.

impact.why: Gold wins back Friday's loss and more as softer oil cools inflation fears.
Australia mines a lot of gold, so a higher price gives its currency slight support.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures, and whether the chance of a December Fed rise moves away from about 80%.

items.headline: Asian stocks bounce after a rough week as the dollar holds its jobs-day gains
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: Asian shares rose on Monday after last week's slide, with Japan's Nikkei up 2.5%. The dollar stayed near the high it reached after Friday's strong US jobs report.

beats.was: Asian stocks fell about 4.6% last week as doubts grew about spending on artificial intelligence, after Democrats' gains in the US midterm elections raised the risk of tighter rules for AI and data centres. Friday's US jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs, twice what was expected.
beats.happened: A broad index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.8%, and Japan's Nikkei and Taiwan's main index each gained about 2.5%. The dollar index held near 102.2 after its biggest one-day gain in five months; the euro was near $1.115 and the dollar near 158.2 yen. Markets now see nearly an 80% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, and New York Fed President John Williams said inflation is still too high.
beats.means: The stock bounce eases some of last week's fear, but it is a pause, not a turn, and the dollar's support from expected Fed rate rises is still in place ahead of Tuesday's US inflation figures.
beats.fx: Calmer stock markets help risk-sensitive currencies like the Australian dollar and take a little away from the yen and franc. A Fed that keeps raising rates keeps the dollar firm against most of them.

impact.why: The dollar keeps its jobs-day gain as bets on a December Fed rise stay near 80%.
A rebound in Asian stocks gives risk-sensitive currencies some relief.
Calmer markets reduce the pull of the yen as a safe place to park money.

items.watch: Tuesday's US October inflation figures, and whether Asian stocks hold the bounce.

items.headline: Drone attack halts Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and cuts power to most of Kurdistan
items.story_title: Gulf: attacks spread beyond Hormuz
items.summary: A drone hit a gas storage site at Khor Mor, one of the biggest gas fields in Iraq's Kurdish region, on Sunday night, stopping production. About 70% of the region lost power.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran for months, and attacks have spread beyond the Strait of Hormuz to sites across the Gulf, including a Houthi strike on Riyadh over the weekend. Khor Mor was also hit in November 2025.
beats.happened: An explosive-laden drone struck the field's gas storage on Sunday night and started a fire. The Kurdish electricity ministry said 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of power went off the grid. No group has claimed it; security sources quoted by Reuters suspect Iran or allied Iraqi militias. It came hours after US President Donald Trump said new US strikes on Iran are unlikely while talks go on.
beats.means: Khor Mor's gas feeds local power plants, not export markets, so the direct hit to world energy supply is small. The bigger signal is that attacks on energy sites keep happening even as Washington and Tehran talk about a deal.
beats.fx: It adds a little to war risk, which supports oil, gold and the Swiss franc, but on its own it is not enough to move currencies much.

impact.why: Another strike on a Gulf energy site keeps war risk alive, though this gas is used locally, not exported.
Fresh attacks keep some safe-haven demand for the franc.

items.watch: Whether anyone claims the attack, and whether strikes on energy sites in Iraq and the Gulf keep coming during the US-Iran talks.

items.headline: Oil slips as trading opens for the week after Trump says new Iran strikes are unlikely
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil fell as Asian trading opened on Monday, with Brent down about 0.6% to near $97.70 a barrel. It came after US President Donald Trump said fresh attacks on Iran are very unlikely if a strong deal is signed.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, and the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil, is still largely shut. Brent crude fell about 13% last week, to near $98, on hopes the war is winding down.
beats.happened: At Monday's open in Asia, Brent dropped 64 cents to about $97.70 and briefly lost more than $1, while US crude (WTI) slipped 35 cents to about $90.50. Traders were reacting to Trump telling CNN on Sunday that new US strikes are very unlikely if Iran signs a strong agreement. Both sides also reported ships hit in or near the strait over the weekend.
beats.means: The market's first move of the week leans toward the hope of a deal rather than the weekend ship attacks. The drop is small, so the war premium in oil is easing, not gone.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps big energy importers like Japan and the euro area and takes a little support from oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar. It also trims the safe-haven bid that war fears give gold and the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Brent opens the week lower as softer US war talk eases fear of new supply losses.
Canada earns a lot from oil, so a lower price takes a little support from its currency.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so cheaper oil eases the drain on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the draft deal from the Qatar talks, and whether ship attacks near Hormuz keep coming.

items.headline: The New Zealand dollar edges up after the election, though the final result is weeks away
items.story_title: New Zealand election: who governs next
items.summary: The New Zealand dollar rose about 0.5% in the first trading after Saturday's election, which leaves Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's bloc just ahead but with about 400,000 votes still to count.

beats.was: New Zealand voted on Saturday, November 7. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon leads a three-party government of his National Party, ACT and New Zealand First.
beats.happened: The early count gives Luxon's bloc 67 of 131 seats, one more than it needs to govern, against 57 for Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. National's own vote fell to about 29% from about 38% in 2023, and Finance Minister Nicola Willis lost her seat. The final count is due on November 27.
beats.means: The current government looks likely to stay, so economic policy probably won't change much. But the margin is thin, special votes could shift it, and coalition talks could drag on.
beats.fx: The small rise came in thin early trading and looks more like relief than a firm verdict. Until the count settles, the US dollar, global mood and Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate bets matter more.

impact.why: A likely continuity government takes away some political risk, though the final count could still change it.

items.watch: The official result on November 27, and whether special votes cost Luxon's bloc its majority.

items.headline: Iran's foreign minister says its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days still stands
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran's offer to the US, which would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, is still on the table. He said the decision now sits with the White House, and warned Iran would hit back if the US chose war.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, and the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, is close to shut. Through mediators in Qatar, Iran has offered a two-day plan: the US eases its naval blockade and frees some Iranian money, and Iran lets ships through Hormuz again.
beats.happened: Araghchi wrote on X on Sunday evening that the offer remains in force. He said US voters had already spoken in last week's midterm elections, so it is now up to the White House, and he set an end to fighting on all fronts as part of the terms. He also warned of a military answer if Washington picks war. The US has not publicly replied.
beats.means: Both sides are now saying the door is open: President Trump said earlier on Sunday new strikes are unlikely while talks progress. That keeps a deal possible, but nothing is agreed and Iran's terms go wider than Hormuz.
beats.fx: Any real sign the strait could reopen would pull oil lower and help energy importers such as Japan and the euro area. Until the US answers, the risk of more fighting keeps some support under oil, gold and the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran repeats it could reopen Hormuz in two days, but the offer is not new and the US has not replied.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so a path to cheaper oil helps the yen a little.
Canada exports oil, so talk of more supply getting through weighs slightly on its currency.

items.watch: A public US reply to the two-day offer, or fresh attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: A record 1.28 billion barrels of oil sit on tankers at sea as the Hormuz shutdown snarls shipping
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Crude held on tankers has hit a record of about 1.28 billion barrels, up roughly 16%, as the Iran war forces longer routes and slower transfers. Shipping now makes up a far bigger share of what a barrel costs.

beats.was: With the Strait of Hormuz largely shut by the Iran war, oil from the Gulf has to take longer, costlier paths, and countries have drawn down their stored oil. Brent crude fell sharply last week to near $98 a barrel on hopes the war is ending.
beats.happened: A market newsletter, The Kobeissi Letter, counts a record 1.28 billion barrels of crude on ships, up from about 1.1 billion. The head of Abu Dhabi's state oil company, Sultan Al Jaber, said earlier this month that shipping has risen from under 5% to over 30% of a barrel's cost, and that close to a billion barrels have come out of global stocks.
beats.means: A lot of oil is in transit rather than reaching refineries quickly, while stockpiles are thinner. That keeps supply fragile even if prices dipped last week.
beats.fx: This adds to the case that oil stays costly, which tends to help oil exporters like Canada and hurt big importers like Japan. It is a background figure rather than fresh news, so the push is mild.

impact.why: Thinner stockpiles and slow shipping keep supply tight beneath last week's price drop.
Canada sells a lot of oil abroad, so costly oil supports its currency.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so higher costs weigh on the yen.

items.watch: Whether tankers start moving through Hormuz again, and how fast global oil stocks are being drawn down.

items.headline: US October inflation figures on Tuesday are the week's big test for a December Fed rate rise
items.story_title: Fed: will it raise rates in December?
items.summary: US consumer prices for October come out Tuesday, with forecasters expecting a 0.3% monthly rise after 0.6% in September. Markets see about an 80% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates at its December 8–9 meeting.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, has been weighing another rate rise because inflation is still too high. Last Friday's jobs report, with 165,000 new jobs in October, made a December rise look much more likely and gave the dollar its best day since June.
beats.happened: A weekly preview lists the US consumer price index for October on Tuesday, November 10, expected to rise 0.3% on the month, or 0.2% leaving out food and energy. Producer prices follow Friday, and more than a dozen Fed officials speak during the week. US stocks fell about 3% last week on worries about spending on AI data centres.
beats.means: With a December rate rise mostly expected, Tuesday's figures mainly decide whether that view holds. A hot reading would lock it in; a soft one would revive doubts.
beats.fx: This is a preview, not news yet. Inflation at or above forecast would back the dollar and weigh on gold, which pays no interest; a clear miss would do the reverse.

impact.why: The dollar's next move hangs on whether inflation confirms a December rate rise.
Gold usually falls when US rate-rise odds go up and gains when they fade.

items.watch: Tuesday's US consumer price figures against the 0.3% forecast, and what Fed officials say about December afterwards.

items.headline: Trump says new US attacks on Iran are very unlikely as long as peace talks keep moving forward
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US President Donald Trump told CNN on Sunday he is very unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran while talks to end the war make progress. He tied that to Iran signing what he called a very strong agreement.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, with the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil, largely shut. Talks in Qatar have produced a draft deal, but on Friday the US hit an Iranian air-defence site and over the weekend Iran said several tankers caught fire near Hormuz.
beats.happened: In a Sunday phone interview with CNN, Trump said renewed US strikes were very unlikely if negotiations keep progressing, provided Iran agrees to a strong deal. He also said the US has picked out possible targets, including 38 bridges it could destroy within an hour. No agreement has been announced.
beats.means: It is a softer tone than last week's talk of fresh strikes, but it comes with conditions and a clear threat. It lowers the near-term risk of a new round of fighting without settling the war or reopening Hormuz.
beats.fx: Less chance of new strikes takes a little of the war premium out of oil and safe havens like gold and the Swiss franc. Ship attacks near Hormuz pull the other way, so Monday's reopening will show which weighs more.

impact.why: Fewer odds of new US strikes ease some fear of fresh supply losses, though nothing is signed.
Calmer war talk trims demand for the franc as a safe place to park money.
Gold loses a little of its war-risk support if strikes look less likely.
Cheaper oil helps Japan, which imports almost all of its energy, but calmer markets cut safe-haven demand for the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the draft deal from the Qatar talks, and any new attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three more tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The naval arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers exploded and burned in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday morning after using a route Iran had not approved. It warned other ships working with US forces would meet the same end.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February. Iran lets ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, only on routes it approves, while the US blockades Iran's ports and escorts tankers through. Oil fell about 13% last week on hopes of a deal, and on Saturday two tankers were reported hit by mines.
beats.happened: On Sunday the Guards' navy said three tankers had exploded and caught fire since early morning on an unapproved channel, with smoke covering the strait. It said the ships had switched off their tracking systems and were helped by the US military, and it did not name them. Separately, a British shipping-safety agency reported tanker incidents off Oman on Saturday, and UAE state media said 22 people were rescued from a burning ship in the Gulf of Oman.
beats.means: Ship attacks near Hormuz are picking up, not easing, just as Iran weighs Qatar's plan to reopen the strait. Iran is signalling that US-escorted traffic will stay a target until a deal is done.
beats.fx: When markets reopen Sunday evening, more burning tankers add to the case for oil to win back some of last week's drop. That tends to help the Canadian dollar, gold and the franc, and weigh on the yen, since Japan imports nearly all its oil.

impact.why: Five tankers reported hit in two days puts supply risk back in the oil price after a 13% weekly fall.
A higher oil bill weighs on Japan, which buys almost all its oil abroad.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.
More attacks at sea tend to draw safe-haven money to the franc.
Gold usually gains when the war looks set to drag on.

items.watch: How far oil rebounds when trading reopens Sunday evening, and whether Iran answers Qatar's plan before more ships are hit.

items.headline: Saudi Aramco's office tower in Riyadh is damaged as Saudi Arabia shoots down Houthi missiles from Yemen
items.story_title: Gulf: attacks spread beyond Hormuz
items.summary: Debris from intercepted missiles blew out windows in Saudi Aramco's tower in Riyadh on Sunday. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said damage was minor and no one was hurt; oil output was not reported affected.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are allied with Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, and an Aramco site south of Riyadh was set on fire in early October. Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil exporter, and Aramco is its state oil company.
beats.happened: On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down several ballistic and cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh, the south of the country and the Eastern Province, where most Saudi oil is produced. Falling debris hit Aramco's office tower in Riyadh's financial district. The Houthis said they had targeted Aramco sites, Riyadh airport and military bases; that claim has not been checked.
beats.means: The war is reaching the Gulf's biggest oil producer, not just ships near Hormuz. This time the damage was to an office, not to wells or export terminals.
beats.fx: It adds a little to the supply worries already lifting oil before markets reopen Sunday evening. That leans toward the Canadian dollar and gold, and against the yen, as Japan imports nearly all its oil.

impact.why: Missiles aimed at Saudi oil areas raise supply worries, though no output was lost.
The war spreading to Saudi Arabia keeps safe-haven demand for gold alive.
Any lift to oil prices raises Japan's import bill.

items.watch: Whether the Houthis hit Saudi oil sites or export terminals, rather than offices; damage to production would be a much bigger deal for oil.

items.headline: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they have dropped their own 2,000 km limit on missile range
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: A spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the country no longer holds itself to a 2,000 km cap on how far its ballistic missiles can fly. Iran is not known to have longer-range missiles yet, so for now this is a threat more than a new capability.

beats.was: For years Iran said it kept its ballistic missiles to a range of about 2,000 km, roughly enough to reach Israel and US bases in the Gulf but not Europe. The country has been at war with the US for months, and Iran's supreme leader recently warned any threat would be met with a response without geographic limits.
beats.happened: At a news conference in Tehran, Revolutionary Guards spokesman General Hossein Mohebbi said the cap has been lifted. He gave no sign that a longer-range missile exists, and outside experts say none is known. US officials have warned before that Iran's space-rocket work could be turned toward longer-range missiles.
beats.means: It is a harder tone at the same time as Iran says its peace offer stands, so it reads as pressure on Washington rather than a change on the ground. It adds to the worry that the war could widen if talks fail.
beats.fx: Tougher talk from Tehran keeps some war-risk support under oil, gold and the Swiss franc. With no new weapon shown, the effect is small next to whether the talks deliver a deal.

impact.why: A harder line from Iran's military adds to the risk the war drags on, though nothing changed on the ground.
More war worry tends to send some money to the franc for safety.
Gold gains a little support from higher war risk.

items.watch: Any Iranian test of a longer-range missile, or whether the threat fades if the Qatar talks produce a deal.

items.headline: The Australian dollar ends the week below 69 US cents, the weakest major currency, despite a rate rise
items.story_title: Australian dollar: rate rise vs global sell-off
items.summary: The Australian dollar lost about 2.4% last week to near 68.7 US cents, its first weekly close below 69 cents since July. Only the Swiss franc gained against the US dollar.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia, the country's central bank, raised its main rate on Tuesday to 4.85%, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008. A higher rate usually helps a currency.
beats.happened: A weekly currency wrap shows the Australian dollar fell the most of the major currencies anyway. A crash in US chip stocks hit risk appetite, and a strong US jobs report on Friday lifted the US dollar. The bank also said growth has slowed and house prices are down nearly 5% from their March peak.
beats.means: The rate rise was outweighed by a global flight from risk. The bank's softer view of growth also hints the run of rises may be near its end.
beats.fx: Headline pressure on the Australian dollar stays down while stocks are shaky and US rates look set to rise. The Swiss franc, the week's only gainer against the US dollar, shows where nervous money went.

impact.why: A global stock sell-off and a stronger US dollar outweighed the Reserve Bank's rate rise.
The franc was the only major currency to gain on the US dollar last week as investors sought safety.

items.watch: Whether US stocks steady this week, and Tuesday's US inflation figures, which could push the US dollar further either way.

items.headline: Blasts reported near the Strait of Hormuz and two tankers hit mines, as the US widens its blockade of Iran to land routes
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island and at the port of Jask on Saturday, and Iran's military said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines. The US set up a new task force to stop Iranian trade over land, while Iran studies Qatar's peace proposals.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut, while the US blockades Iran's ports. Oil fell about 13% last week on hopes of a deal, and on Friday President Trump said US forces made a small new strike on an Iranian air defense site.
beats.happened: On Saturday evening Iranian state media reported two blasts on Qeshm Island and several at Jask, with the cause unclear. Iran's military said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines on a route it had not approved, and the US military said it disabled a ship in the Gulf of Oman that ignored warnings. US Central Command launched Task Force Iron Gate to block weapons and sanctioned goods moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it no longer limits the range of its missiles. Iran is still reviewing proposals carried by Qatar, but officials say it won't discuss its nuclear program until the US meets several conditions.
beats.means: The weekend brought more pressure from both sides, not less: mines and ship incidents near Hormuz, a wider US blockade, and tougher talk from Tehran, while the Qatari plan is still only under review.
beats.fx: Markets reopen Sunday evening. Tankers hitting mines and a tighter blockade could push oil back up after last week's big drop, which tends to help the Canadian dollar and safe havens like the franc and gold, and hurt oil importers like Japan.

impact.why: Tankers hitting mines near Hormuz and a wider US blockade add back supply risk after a 13% weekly fall.
Rising war risk tends to draw safe-haven money to the franc.
Gold usually gains when the war looks set to drag on.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a higher oil bill weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran accepts the Qatari first steps, which would reopen Hormuz in exchange for the US easing its blockade, or whether more ships are hit before markets reopen.

items.headline: New Zealand's election ends nearly tied: Labour edges the party vote, but Prime Minister Luxon's bloc holds a one-seat majority
items.story_title: New Zealand election: who governs next
items.summary: Labour won 29.4% of the party vote against National's 29.2% in Saturday's preliminary count, but National, ACT and NZ First together hold 67 of 131 seats, one more than needed. About 400,000 special votes are still to come, with the official result on November 27.

beats.was: Christopher Luxon's National Party has led a three-party government with ACT and NZ First since 2023. Polls before Saturday's vote showed a close race with Chris Hipkins' Labour, and unemployment is at its highest since 2015.
beats.happened: The Electoral Commission's election-night count, covering almost all ordinary votes, put Labour narrowly ahead on the party vote, 29.36% to 29.21%. On seats, National won 42 and Labour 36; with the Greens on 16, ACT 13, NZ First 12 and Te Pāti Māori 5, Luxon's three-party bloc has 67 seats, one over the 66 needed. The new Opportunity party passed the 5% bar and wins 7 seats. About 400,000 special votes remain, and the official count ends November 27. Luxon said National is again the largest party but compromise will be needed; Hipkins said Labour is ready to govern if it gets the chance.
beats.means: The current government is most likely to stay, but its one-seat edge could vanish when special votes are counted, which in past elections have tended to favour the left. That leaves about three weeks of uncertainty over who governs.
beats.fx: Elections rarely move the New Zealand dollar much on their own. A likely return of the same government means little change in policy, but a slim, unsettled outcome is a small extra worry for a currency that was already the weakest of the majors on Friday.

impact.why: The same government looks likely to continue, but its one-seat majority hangs on special votes counted over the next three weeks.

items.watch: The official count on November 27: if special votes cost the right bloc a seat, coalition talks get harder and a change of government becomes possible.

items.headline: Trump says the US carried out new limited strikes on an Iranian air defense site on Friday, while talks continue
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: President Trump said US forces hit an Iranian air defense system on Friday, calling it a minor strike, and said Washington is still talking to Tehran. Iranian state media reported two blasts on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, have kept crude prices high. This week oil fell about 13% on hopes of a deal, and Iran is studying peace proposals carried by Qatar.
beats.happened: Speaking on Friday evening, Trump said the military had knocked out an Iranian anti-aircraft system in a short, limited strike, the first since Tuesday's US midterm elections. Iranian state media reported two explosions on Qeshm Island. Regional officials described a possible first step under the Qatari plan: the US would ease its blockade of Iranian ports and free some frozen funds, and Iran would let nuclear inspectors in and reopen Hormuz, though Washington has not agreed to the shipping terms.
beats.means: The US is pairing small military hits with diplomacy rather than choosing one, so the risk of a wider flare-up is back on the table even as the outline of a deal takes shape.
beats.fx: Markets are shut for the weekend. When trading resumes Sunday evening, the strike could add back some of the risk premium oil lost this week and draw some money to havens like the franc and gold, unless talks show clear progress first.

impact.why: A fresh US strike after a week of deal hopes puts supply risk back into crude prices.
More fighting tends to draw safe-haven money to the franc; Trump called the strike minor.
Gold usually gains when war risk rises, though the strike was small.
Dearer oil lifts Canada's export earnings.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the strike, and whether the Qatari first-step plan is confirmed by Washington or Tehran before markets reopen Sunday evening.

items.headline: The dollar heads for its best day since June after strong US jobs data, and two Fed officials lean toward more rate rises
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The dollar index rose about 0.8% on Friday, its biggest one-day gain since mid-June, after a strong US jobs report. Two senior Federal Reserve officials said inflation is still too high, and markets now see about an 80% chance of a December rate rise.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation that dearer oil from the Iran war has pushed up. Earlier this week the dollar slipped after Democrats won control of Congress and a sell-off in AI stocks shook markets.
beats.happened: After the government reported 165,000 new jobs in October, far above the roughly 65,000 expected, the dollar index climbed to about 102.3. New York Fed president John Williams said inflation is too high, and San Francisco Fed president Mary Daly said more rate rises will likely be needed. The 2-year US Treasury yield rose to about 4.52%.
beats.means: Strong hiring plus officials openly talking about further rises make a December Fed rate rise the market's main expectation again, after doubts on Thursday.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates lifted the dollar across the board: the euro fell to about $1.114, the pound to about $1.336 a day after the Bank of England's rate rise, and the yen weakened to about 158.4 per dollar.

impact.why: A jobs beat and Fed officials calling for more rises put a December hike back near 80% odds.
The euro gave back its gains for the week as US rates rose.
The pound slipped despite Thursday's Bank of England rise, as the dollar's pull was stronger.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates weighs on the yen.

items.watch: US October inflation figures, out Tuesday November 10: a soft reading would cool talk of a December Fed rise.

items.headline: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than expected, and unemployment fell to 4.1%
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, almost three times what economists expected, and the jobless rate dipped to 4.1%. Earlier months were also revised up and pay rose 0.4% in the month.

beats.was: US hiring had slowed to a crawl this year, with September first reported at just 29,000 new jobs. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September to fight inflation near 3.7%, and markets were weighing another rise in December after Thursday's stock crash and the Democrats' win in Congress.
beats.happened: The government's monthly jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs in October against about 60,000 expected, led by business services and health care. August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000, unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, and average hourly pay rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% on the year.
beats.means: The US job market is much firmer than it looked, and faster pay growth adds to inflation worries. That makes it harder for the Fed to skip a December rate rise.
beats.fx: Strong jobs and firmer pay point to higher US rates for longer, which supports the dollar against the euro, yen and franc and tends to weigh on gold, which pays no interest.

impact.why: Jobs came in near three times the forecast, with upward revisions and faster pay, backing a December Fed rise.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
A wider gap between US and Japanese rates tends to pull the yen lower.

items.watch: How far markets raise the odds of a December Fed rate rise, and whether Fed officials point to this report in coming speeches.
